blocks.text: Why Word still matters for grant writers on Mac

Many grant writers still draft in Word. Instrumentl's March 2026 survey of 1,031 grant professionals found that 84% use word-processing documents. The survey is non-probability, and Instrumentl sells grant software. Treat it as a directional benchmark, not a census.
The same survey found that 68% keep grant documents in email folders. That is the real system of record for many teams. Word files travel as attachments, get renamed, and multiply in inboxes.

Word earns its place for a simple reason. Narrative sections, letters of support, and budget justifications are long documents with headings, tables, and comments. A web form handles those poorly. A Word file handles them well, as long as you set it up with care.
Set up one master file before you write a sentence

Start with a master file for each proposal. Put the funder's rules on the first page, above the title. Copy that file for every draft. Do not start from an old proposal and hope its formatting still fits.

Use styles, not manual formatting. Select a heading, then choose a style from Home > Styles. When every heading uses one style, you can change the look of the whole document in one move. Hand-made bold and font size changes do not travel well.

Build a short checklist on that first page. Write down the page limit, the font, the margins, the character limits, and the file type. Delete the checklist before you export, or move it to a notes file so it never reaches the funder.

items: Page limit, and whether it counts attachments and appendices
Required font, size, and margin rules, if the funder sets them
Character limit for each portal text field
Accepted file type, such as PDF or plain text
Deadline, with the time zone the portal uses

blocks.text: A master file also protects your numbers. When the team agrees on budget totals, write them once in the spreadsheet and paste them into the file. Copy-paste errors multiply fast when three people edit the same figure.
Captions and cross-references: the numbering traps

Let Word number your captions. Select the figure or table, then go to References > Insert Caption. Choose the label, such as Figure or Table. Word inserts a sequential number as a field, not as typed text.
The trap comes after an edit. Word numbers a new caption when you insert it. When you delete or move a caption, the numbers can go stale until you update them. Word does not always do that for you.

Microsoft's caption guide says to select the whole document, then press F9 or choose Update Field. On a Mac, press ⌘A to select everything, then press Fn+F9. On many Mac keyboards, F9 needs the Fn key. Microsoft's guide lists Windows keys, so check the Mac keys on your own build.
A worked example helps. Say you have Figures 1 to 5 in a grant. You delete Figure 2. Word may still show 1, 3, 4, and 5 until you update. After ⌘A and Fn+F9, the captions read 1 to 4.

Then fix every in-text mention. A sentence that says see Figure 4 must point at the right caption. If you typed that number by hand, it will not change. Use a cross-reference from the References tab instead, so the text updates with the caption.

rows: A caption was deleted or moved
Press ⌘A, then Fn+F9 to update the fields
Text says Figure 4, but the caption says Figure 3
The in-text number was typed by hand
Replace it with a cross-reference from References
Each caption was formatted by hand
Change the Caption style once, not each caption

blocks.text: Budget tables without the math errors

Build the budget in a spreadsheet. Word tables hold numbers, but they do not check your math the way Excel or Numbers does. Do the arithmetic where it is safe, then paste the finished table into Word as a table.

Instrumentl's 2026 survey found that only 18% of grant professionals can answer a basic budget question within minutes. Many teams keep the numbers in one file and the justification in another. Name both files with the same proposal code, so nobody searches for the wrong one.

Compare totals before every send. Check the Word table total against the spreadsheet total. One wrong digit in a total can reach a reviewer. Make the comparison a fixed step in your submission checklist.

Write each budget justification as plain sentences. Name the item, the amount, and the reason it is needed. Reviewers read those sentences closely, and a clear sentence is harder to misread than a table cell.
Funder text fields: paste plain text, not styled Word text

Many funder portals accept plain text only. NIH's rules for text fields say bold, bullets, and subscript or superscript are lost when you paste from Word. Plan for that loss before deadline week, not during it.

NIH also counts spaces and punctuation against its character limits. Check the count in Word with Review > Word Count, and read the character figure that includes spaces. The portal's own counter has the final say, so compare the two before you submit.

NIH recommends straight quotes. Pasting from Word can turn straight quotes into smart quotes. NIH also says to replace em dashes with shorter dashes. These small changes can show up as odd symbols in the portal.

blocks.title: Plain text route
blocks.text: Write in Word, copy the text, and paste it into TextEdit. Then choose Format > Make Plain Text, or press ⇧⌘T. Copy from TextEdit into the portal, and recount the characters there.
This route takes about a minute per field. It prevents the bad surprise of a broken bullet or an odd symbol after you submit. Use it for every text field, even the short ones.
Templates, page limits, and rules that change

A good template saves hours. Build one proposal template with your styles, margins, caption style, and heading numbers already set. Save it as a Word template file, then open a fresh copy for each application.

Funder formatting rules change by opportunity. One program asks for a specific font and margin set. Another sets a page limit and says nothing else. Read the current announcement, not last year's guide.

Text fields and page limits need different checks. NIH text fields have no font or margin requirements, because they limit characters rather than pages. A narrative in a PDF and a portal text box need different checks.
Keep the funder's exact wording in your master file, next to your checklist. When the portal or the rules change, you can compare the old and new wording in a minute.
Working with reviewers and co-authors in Word

Many grant drafts pass through several hands. Reviewers, finance staff, and a program lead each want changes. Without a clear system, the file name becomes the version history, and that never works for long.

Instrumentl found that 96% of grant professionals rely on at least one workaround. A file name with a date and your initials beats a folder full of copies. Save a new copy at each milestone, not at each edit.

Use Word comments for questions about a specific sentence. Keep feedback in the main file, not in a separate email thread. Ask one person to merge the comments, and put the deadline in the first comment.
Track Changes and co-authoring depend on how your team stores the file. Ask your team's IT lead or Microsoft 365 admin how the shared folder works before you rely on either feature.
The Copilot button in Word for Mac: what changed in 2026
Microsoft added a Copilot Dynamic Action Button to Word. It sits in a consistent corner in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint on Windows, Mac, and the web. Only people with Copilot access see it.

Microsoft says the rollout began in April 2026 and was due to finish by June 2026. On a Mac, the Move to ribbon option needs macOS build 16.109.525.2 or later. Microsoft says your choice is remembered for each app.

Sources disagree on what you get. Office Watch reported in June 2026 that Microsoft delivered Move to upper corner in its Microsoft 365 for Mac tests, and that the button cannot be fully turned off. Microsoft's page says clearing the Enable Copilot checkbox hides Copilot entry points for personal accounts. Check your own build and settings before you plan around either.
To focus the button from the keyboard, press ⌘⌃I. Microsoft lists that shortcut for Mac. Keep the button out of the way while you write, and turn it back on when you need it.
What Lazur does in Word, and what it leaves to you
Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud, and it can point at the thing you are looking for.

Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click. Lazur does not click buttons or edit your files for you.

Dictation uses a different key. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation is unlimited on both Pro and Power, and it works well for the narrative section you keep putting off.

Snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots help with grant boilerplate. Save your organization's legal name, address, and standard paragraphs as snippets. Add unusual program names to the dictionary, so dictation keeps the spelling right.
Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report. Use it to gather a funder's current rules, then open the official announcement yourself and check the details.
Mistakes grant writers make in Word on Mac

items: Typing caption numbers by hand, then wondering why they stop matching
Pasting straight from Word into a portal text field
Keeping budget math in Word, then finding a total is off
Naming files final, final2, with no date or initials
Trusting last year's page limit or font rule
Skipping a last read of the exported PDF

blocks.text: Each mistake costs time you cannot get back. Instrumentl's survey found that 87% of grant professionals have walked away from, delayed, or downsized a grant because of operational burden. The survey does not single out Word. It does show how much burden grant teams carry.
How much time proposals take

A PLOS ONE survey of 195 academics found that an average proposal took 116 hours of PI time. The study covered 113 astronomers and 82 psychologists, and its figures date from 2015. It does not describe grant writers in general.

The same study found that hours spent writing were not related to whether a grant was funded. More writing time did not predict a win. Time spent on setup and checks may matter more, but that is a judgment, not a finding.

Instrumentl reports that a typical grant professional spends 29.5 hours a week on manual, repetitive tasks. That figure covers all such tasks, not Word alone. It still shows why a clean setup pays off across a whole year.
Your next steps before the next deadline

items: Build the master file with styles and a checklist on page one.
Move every caption to References > Insert Caption, then update with ⌘A and Fn+F9.
Replace typed figure numbers in the text with cross-references.
Build the budget in a spreadsheet, then compare totals before each send.
Test one portal text field through TextEdit before deadline week.

faq.question: Does Word for Mac work for grant applications?
faq.answer: Yes, for most narrative drafts, budget justifications, and letters. Many grant writers draft there first. Portals can still strip formatting, so check each text field and the exported file before you submit.

faq.question: Why do my caption numbers stop matching in Word for Mac?
faq.answer: Word numbers new captions automatically. After you delete or move a caption, select the whole document with ⌘A and press Fn+F9 to update the fields. Then check every in-text reference, because typed numbers do not update.

faq.question: Can I paste Word text into an NIH text field?
faq.answer: You can, but NIH says text fields accept plain text only. Bold, bullets, and subscript or superscript are lost. Paste through TextEdit with Format > Make Plain Text first, then recount the characters in the portal.

faq.question: Does Lazur write my grant for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides, points, explains, answers out loud, and drafts and types text. It does not click buttons or edit your files for you. You still write, check, and submit the proposal.

faq.question: Where is the Copilot button in Word on a Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft places it in a consistent corner of Word, and only people with Copilot access see it. Press ⌘⌃I to focus it. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask Lazur where it is, and Lazur circles it on screen.

faq.question: How much time do grant proposals take?
faq.answer: A 2015 PLOS ONE survey of 195 academics found an average of 116 hours of PI time per proposal. That study covered astronomers and psychologists, not grant writers in general, so use it as a rough reference only.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a Mac app for macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel. Windows is planned, but it is not available.
